body: {"total":7,"records":[{"title":"Clinical decision support for diagnostic imaging orders: a systematic review of effects on appropriateness and volume","authors":"Okafor-Lindahl P, Brandt-Nakamura S, Idowu-Fischer R","year":2018,"venue":"Journal of Imaging Quality and Safety","doi":"10.5555/jiqs.2018.0442","providerType":"systematic review","abstract":"We included 32 studies of electronic clinical decision support at the point of ordering diagnostic imaging, 6 of them randomised. Across 14 studies that reported appropriateness, the proportion of inappropriate orders fell by a pooled relative 27 percent (95 percent CI 18 to 35 percent). Effects on imaging volume were smaller and inconsistent. Studies in which clinicians could ignore the advice without giving a reason showed smaller effects. Few studies reported patient outcomes, and most were uncontrolled before-after comparisons from academic centres. We rated the certainty of the evidence as low."},{"title":"Decision support for lumbar spine imaging in adults with low back pain: a systematic review and meta-analysis","authors":"Ferreira-Holm K, Achebe-Tanaka L, Morrow-Singh V","year":2021,"venue":"Spine Imaging Evidence","doi":"10.5555/sie.2021.0113","providerType":"meta-analysis","abstract":"We included 11 studies of decision support for lumbar spine imaging in adults presenting with low back pain in primary care or emergency departments. Decision support reduced lumbar imaging orders for non-specific low back pain (risk ratio 0.78, 95 percent CI 0.66 to 0.92). Of the included studies, 2 randomised trials measured pain and function at 3 months and found no differences between groups. Heterogeneity was substantial, largely explained by whether the tool required a reason to override. No study reported outcomes by socioeconomic group or language."},{"title":"Interventions to reduce low-value imaging for low back pain: an overview of reviews","authors":"Lindqvist-Obi M, Carrasco-Hughes D","year":2016,"venue":"Musculoskeletal Care Reviews","doi":"10.5555/mcr.2016.0058","providerType":"review","abstract":"We identified 9 reviews of interventions to reduce imaging for low back pain. Audit and feedback, decision support at ordering and targeted education were the interventions with the most consistent reductions in imaging. Confidence in the reviews was low: 4 of the 9 reviews were rated critically low on a standard appraisal tool, mainly because they did not assess risk of bias in included studies. The overview did not account for primary studies included in more than one review and did not report patient outcomes."},{"title":"Override of imaging decision support advice by clinicians: a systematic review","authors":"Hassan-Whitfield J, Obuya-Lund R","year":2023,"venue":"Health Informatics Practice","providerType":"systematic review","abstract":"We reviewed 19 studies that reported how often clinicians overrode imaging decision support advice. Override rates ranged from 49 to 96 percent of alerts that advised against an order. Overrides were more frequent when alerts fired for orders already judged urgent, when the tool gave no alternative, and in emergency departments. Tools that required a structured reason to override had lower override rates. Few studies examined whether overridden orders were later judged appropriate, and none measured effects on patients whose orders were cancelled after an alert."},{"title":"Imaging for low back pain in adults: clinical practice guideline","authors":"Low Back Pain Guideline Development Group","year":2019,"venue":"Clinical Guidance Series in Imaging","doi":"10.5555/cgsi.2019.0007","providerType":"practice guideline","abstract":"The guideline recommends against routine imaging for adults with low back pain without red flags, and against imaging within the first six weeks for non-specific pain. Imaging is recommended for suspected cauda equina syndrome, malignancy, infection or fracture, and for radiculopathy persisting after six weeks when surgery or injection is being considered. The guideline notes that imaging without an indication is associated with more further investigation and treatment without better outcomes. Evidence was graded low to moderate for most recommendations."},{"title":"Methodological quality and overlap of systematic reviews of imaging decision support: an appraisal with AMSTAR 2","authors":"Petersen-Oyelaran A, Kim-Castellanos T","year":2024,"venue":"Research Synthesis Methods in Radiology","doi":"10.5555/rsmr.2024.0019","providerType":"journal-article","abstract":"We appraised 26 systematic reviews of decision support for imaging orders with AMSTAR 2. Confidence was rated critically low for 15 reviews and low for 7, most often because protocols were not registered and excluded studies were not listed. The primary studies overlapped substantially across reviews, with a corrected covered area of 18 percent, so counting reviews would double-count the same evidence. Reviews that reported larger effects more often included uncontrolled studies. The authors recommend overlap matrices and AMSTAR 2 ratings in any overview."},{"title":"Do imaging stewardship interventions affect groups differently? A scoping review of equity reporting","authors":"Mahlangu-Reid C, Soto-Brennan P, Fitzgerald-Ude N","year":2020,"venue":"Equity in Health Services","providerType":"journal-article","abstract":"We mapped 38 studies of interventions to reduce low-value imaging and recorded whether they reported effects by socioeconomic position, ethnicity, language, age or sex. Only 4 of 38 studies reported any subgroup effect, and none reported effects by language. Two studies found that reductions in imaging were smaller among patients from deprived areas, while one found no difference. Most studies were from academic centres in high-income settings. The review concludes that the equity effects of imaging stewardship are largely unknown and recommends routine subgroup reporting."}]}
